verses.text: When we had escaped, then they  learned that the island was called Malta.
The natives showed us uncommon kindness; for they kindled a fire, and received us all, because of the present rain, and because of the cold.
But when Paul had gathered a bundle of sticks and laid them on the fire, a viper came out because of the heat, and fastened on his hand.
When the natives saw the creature hanging from his hand, they said to one another, “No doubt this man is a murderer, whom, though he has escaped from the sea, yet Justice has not allowed to live.”
However he shook off the creature into the fire, and wasn’t harmed.

But they expected that he would have swollen or fallen down dead suddenly, but when they watched for a long time and saw nothing bad happen to him, they changed their minds, and said that he was a god.
Now in the neighborhood of that place were lands belonging to the chief man of the island, named Publius, who received us, and courteously entertained us for three days.
The father of Publius lay sick of fever and dysentery. Paul entered in to him, prayed, and laying his hands on him, healed him.
Then when this was done, the rest also who had diseases in the island came, and were cured.
They also honored us with many honors, and when we sailed, they put on board the things that we needed.
After three months, we set sail in a ship of Alexandria which had wintered in the island, whose sign was “The Twin Brothers.”
Touching at Syracuse, we stayed there three days.
From there we circled around and arrived at Rhegium. After one day, a south wind sprang up, and on the second day we came to Puteoli,
where we found brothers,  and were entreated to stay with them for seven days. So we came to Rome.
From there the brothers, when they heard of us, came to meet us as far as The Market of Appius and The Three Taverns. When Paul saw them, he thanked God, and took courage.
When we entered into Rome, the centurion delivered the prisoners to the captain of the guard, but Paul was allowed to stay by himself with the soldier who guarded him.

After three days Paul called together those who were the leaders of the Jews. When they had come together, he said to them, “I, brothers, though I had done nothing against the people, or the customs of our fathers, still was delivered prisoner from Jerusalem into the hands of the Romans,
who, when they had examined me, desired to set me free, because there was no cause of death in me.
But when the Jews spoke against it, I was constrained to appeal to Caesar, not that I had anything about which to accuse my nation.
For this cause therefore I asked to see you and to speak with you. For because of the hope of Israel I am bound with this chain.”
They said to him, “We neither received letters from Judea concerning you, nor did any of the brothers come here and report or speak any evil of you.
But we desire to hear from you what you think. For, as concerning this sect, it is known to us that everywhere it is spoken against.”

When they had appointed him a day, many people came to him at his lodging. He explained to them, testifying about God’s Kingdom, and persuading them concerning Jesus, both from the law of Moses and from the prophets, from morning until evening.
Some believed the things which were spoken, and some disbelieved.
When they didn’t agree among themselves, they departed after Paul had spoken one word, “The Holy Spirit spoke rightly through Isaiah, the prophet, to our fathers,
saying, ‘Go to this people, and say, in hearing, you will hear, but will in no way understand. In seeing, you will see, but will in no way perceive.

For this people’s heart has grown callous. Their ears are dull of hearing. Their eyes they have closed. Lest they should see with their eyes, hear with their ears, understand with their heart, and would turn again, and I would heal them.’
“Be it known therefore to you, that the salvation of God is sent to the nations, and they will listen.”
When he had said these words, the Jews departed, having a great dispute among themselves.
Paul stayed two whole years in his own rented house, and received all who were coming to him,
preaching God’s Kingdom, and teaching the things concerning the Lord Jesus Christ with all boldness, without hindrance.

footnotes.content: After the storm, they reach solid ground—Malta. I notice how the Lord's mercy meets us not in a city we planned, but on an island we never expected. Safe harbor often looks different from what we imagined.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: These strangers—these "natives" to whom Luke says we are nothing—kindle a fire and shelter us from the rain and cold. Uncommon kindness: the Lord's face often meets us through the hands of those we've never met.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Paul gathers sticks for the fire, a small mercy work. Then the viper—heat draws it out, and it fastens to his hand. Even in shelter, danger coils in the warmth.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Justice has not allowed him to live"—how quick we are to read God's judgment in suffering. The Maltese see the snake and conclude Paul deserves it. We do the same, don't we? Reading God's mind in misfortune.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He shakes the creature into the fire and is unharmed. Not a showy miracle—practical, ordinary—yet it speaks louder than words. The Lord keeps those He intends to use.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They expected him to swell or fall dead. Instead, watching and waiting, they change their minds—from "murderer" to "god." Sometimes one small kindness, sustained through doubt, reshapes how people see.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Publius, the chief man, opens his home for three days. A place of honor, a resting place. Notice how the Lord provides not just bare survival, but dignity and care through kindly hands.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Paul enters, prays, lays his hands on Publius's father—fever and dysentery break. Prayer and touch: the old languages of love and healing. The Gospel moves not only through words, but through presence.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Word spreads, and all who are sick on the island come and are cured. One healing opens the door; faithfulness multiplies. The Gospel travels fastest through gratitude.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They honor Paul and the others, loading the ship with provisions for the journey. Gratitude finds a thousand ways to give back. The Gospel doesn't leave people poorer—it leaves them richer in spirit and mercy.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: After three months, they board a ship with the sign "The Twin Brothers"—Castor and Pollux, the pagan protectors of sailors. Luke names it plainly; the Gospel meets people where they are, with the gods they know.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Syracuse: a stop, three days to breathe and stretch. The journey to Rome unfolds in small mercies, one harbor at a time. We often miss God's presence in the rest stops.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Rhegium, then south wind, then Puteoli—real places, real sea-roads to Rome. Luke traces the geography as if each harbor matters, each wind is known. The Lord's Providence works through the ordinary rhythms of travel.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: At Puteoli they find brothers—the Church already waiting. Seven days of fellowship, then onward to Rome. The body of Christ is not confined to one city; it reaches to the ends of the earth.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Roman brothers hear and come out to meet Paul—The Market of Appius, The Three Taverns. When Paul sees them, he thanks God and takes courage. Love recognizes love across any distance.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: In Rome, Paul is allowed to stay in his own rented house with a guard. Not a cell, not chains in darkness, but a house. Even in captivity, the Lord keeps a space open for His messenger.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Paul calls together the Jewish leaders—three days in and already speaking. He speaks plainly of his innocence and his chains. Sometimes boldness means simply telling the truth without embellishment.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Romans examined him and found no cause for death. Paul appeals to a higher truth: his innocence is not an opinion, but a fact. Truth carries its own authority, whether the world recognizes it or not.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Constrained to appeal to Caesar—not from malice toward his nation, but for his own defense. Paul speaks without bitterness, naming the trap he's caught in without hating those who set it. Grace doesn't excuse injustice; it transcends it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Because of the hope of Israel I am bound with this chain." Paul doesn't hide why he suffers. He wears the chain honestly, naming it as the cost of faithfulness. That clarity invites others to choose whether they'll pay it too.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Jewish leaders say they received no letters accusing him, and no report came from Judea. A curiosity—they haven't been briefed against him. The Lord often leaves space for people to meet us without preconceived judgment.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "We desire to hear from you what you think." They know this sect is "spoken against everywhere"—the Way has a reputation. Yet they ask Paul to speak for himself. Open curiosity is sometimes the first crack where truth can enter.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A day appointed; many come. Paul testifies from morning to evening—about God's Kingdom, about Jesus, from Law and Prophets. Long witness, patient witness, speaking truth without rushes. The faithful teacher doesn't look at the clock.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Some believed; some disbelieved. Even Paul's testimony divides. We want to believe our words will win everyone—they won't. The Gospel is true whether the crowd agrees or not.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: As they depart in disagreement, Paul speaks one word—the Holy Spirit spoke rightly through Isaiah. Paul names the prophet, the Word, the ancient voice. Truth doesn't begin with us; it echoes through centuries.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "In hearing, you will hear, but will in no way understand." Isaiah's words about Israel's long refusal. Sometimes people hear the Gospel clearly and still turn away—not from lack of clarity, but from hardness of heart.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Their heart has grown callous, their ears dull, their eyes they have closed." Not a judgment from God alone, but a description of what happens when we turn away again and again. Refusal hardens; resistance builds walls.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "The salvation of God is sent to the nations, and they will listen." When the Jewish leaders turn away, Paul doesn't chase them—he turns toward the Gentiles. The Gospel won't be stopped; it moves to whoever opens a door.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Jews depart, having a great dispute among themselves. Some truth-telling always leaves commotion. Paul doesn't smooth it over or soften the message—he speaks and lets it do its work.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Two whole years Paul stayed in his own rented house, receiving all who came. Not in prison, but not free—in a strange middle ground. Yet he doesn't wait for permission; he opens his doors and speaks.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Preaching God's Kingdom, teaching about Jesus, with all boldness, without hindrance—so Luke ends the Acts. Readers today hear an echo in Paul's final freedom: even when the chains remain, the Word runs free. As of 2026-10, we hear it still.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
